1:
What event the chapter describes is disputed at the outset, and the positions are five. Clarke refers the opening to the destruction of the city by the Romans, and says the prophet passes at once from that tragedy to the extermination of the enemies of Christianity in the latter days. Wesley agrees on the Romans, who then ruled the nations of that part of the world, and identifies the residue as the small number spared by the conqueror. Gill rejects that reading outright: the Romans were not all nations, and at that capture not a part but the whole city went into captivity with none remaining; he prefers the gathering of the kings of the earth to the last battle, or a future dispossession after the Jews have again inhabited the city, and notes that the old Jewish commentators applied it to the times of their Messiah, which he allows if the last times are meant. Calvin sets aside all three readings he knows, that the chapter concerns Antichrist, or the last day, or the destruction under the Roman emperor, and holds that the prophet meant the calamities then at hand, since the city was not yet built and evils continued from the rebuilding until the coming of Christ; his purpose is pastoral, that those who had returned might be prepared for trials and not repent of returning. Henry keeps the Roman reference but makes the point of the passage the alternation itself, that God's providences towards his church are strangely changing, the tide running high against them and then turning.

Two voices work at the opening phrase rather than the event. Ellicott would render it not the day of the Lord but a day coming for the Lord, that is, one on which he will signally manifest his glory, and says the second half of the verse gives with one stroke of the pen the most vivid description of the first feature of that day. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same rendering by the same reasoning, that the day belongs to him not because he brings it to pass but because he will display his glory on it, and add the structure: the day first brings calamity on Israel, and that calamity is the occasion for destroying the enemies and saving the people.

The clause about the residue is where Ellicott makes his hardest objection. He grants that a remnant was left in the Chaldean conquest, and then, rather than decide whether the later capture answers to the prophecy, sets a long passage of the historian before his readers: the soldiers wearied of killing, the order that only those in arms be slain, the aged killed nonetheless, the survivors driven into the temple court and sorted by an officer who put the seditious to death, reserved the tallest for the triumph, sent those above seventeen to the mines or the provincial theatres, and sold the younger for slaves. He then asks the question the catalogue is built to raise, what room is there for a remnant. Clarke and Wesley both take the clause the other way and read it as fulfilled, Clarke observing that many were preserved for slavery and for exhibition in the provincial theatres, and Wesley that the survivors were not forbidden to dwell about the city. Henry reads it as mercy rather than statistics, judgment beginning at the house of God but not ending there nor making a full end, so that a remnant is spared and many receive the gospel. On the going forth of the Lord, Gill identifies the warrior as Christ, Ellicott points to a series of older deliverances where God appeared as champion in the hour of direst need, Wesley places it after the punishment of the Jews is complete, and Clarke, having referred the fighting to the destruction of the Roman empire by northern nations, admits that the place is obscure.
4:
The standing of the feet on the mountain divides the literal from the figurative readers. Gill argues that this cannot refer to the destruction of the city, since no such appearance occurred then, and takes it of a future descent to the very spot from which the ascension took place; he also reports a Jewish notion that at the resurrection the mountain will cleave and those buried in other countries be rolled through the caverns of the earth to emerge beneath it. Clarke gives two readings without reconciling them: a conqueror appearing in full possession, God displaying his power in the restoration as at the dividing of the sea; and the observation that some refer the whole to the Roman siege, the mountain being where the general posted his army and a legion from Jericho was stationed, and the same from which the city's destruction was foretold and the ascension made. He then commits to the second and suggests that the removing of half the mountain means the lines of circumvallation, the entrenchments thrown up during the siege, particularly those cut on that mountain. Ellicott says the language is of course figurative, and notes that an earthquake commonly accompanies the Lord's appearing.

The flight to the valley draws the chapter's densest textual note. Ellicott rejects one modern rendering as unsupported by the Hebrew, records that several ancient versions by a different vocalisation read that the valley shall be stopped, and dismisses it as inappropriate; on the place named at the valley's end he reports two locations proposed near the city and a third view that the word is a preposition meaning very nigh. He then takes up the earthquake used as a date, not recorded in the sacred history but leaving so deep an impression that it became an era to reckon from, and cites a modern parallel of events dated by a great earthquake; from which he concludes that the mention does not fix the prophecy to that reign, as some have affirmed, and adds two arguments, that the second person need not address the hearers directly since a nation's continuity allows it to mean the same people earlier, and that the appended royal title might imply hearers needed reminding who he was. He would read the last word as angels rather than saints, and notes that some copies read with him rather than with thee. Clarke mentions a proposal that the valley is the one by which an earlier king attempted escape, thinks the verse speaks only of the Roman wars, and admits the name is unknown. Gill and Wesley keep to the shelter, a refuge from the glory of his majesty.

The strange light of the following verses is read three ways. Clarke takes the mixture metaphorically, justice and mercy together with more light than darkness because mercy triumphs over judgment, and Wesley says the same, some mercy allaying the bitterness of judgment. Ellicott will not have the mixture and re-renders the clause, that there shall not be light and the glorious ones, meaning the heavenly bodies, shall fail, the word signifying literally to become coagulated; the state is not a mixture but a murky gloom like a desert sand-storm. Keil and Delitzsch translate similarly, no light and the glorious ones melting away. On the single day, Gill notes it will not continue long, Wesley makes it one continued day with no setting sun, and Ellicott calls it an extraordinary and unique day, citing two parallels for the idiom. All agree on the close: Clarke has the gospel light going out from the city at the end of the visitation, and Ellicott draws the structural point, that as the darkest hour precedes the dawn the climax of need is the precursor of God's saving power, this half-verse standing to what precedes as the earlier promise of the Lord going forth stood to the capture of the city.
8:
The living waters are read spiritually by everyone, and the differences lie in what is stressed. Gill develops the figure, calling them living because they quicken dead sinners and revive drooping saints, and running because of the swiftness and force and spread of the doctrine; the city they issue from he takes either literally, as rebuilt at the conversion of the Jews, or mystically as the church. Clarke turns the figure into a route, the knowledge going out by apostles to the neighbouring lands, then to Greece and Italy and the isles. Henry adds a date, that the city was made a spring of living waters when the Spirit was poured out on the apostles, and observes that where the gospel goes with the graces of the Spirit the country is watered as well as the city. On the two seas the voices agree that the eastern and western are meant, Ellicott adding that these boundaries denote the whole of the land, and Keil and Delitzsch rendering the halves as flowing into each. On summer and winter, Clarke says the stream shall never cease, Ellicott that it shall be perennial and not dry up as the eastern watercourses do, and Wesley that these waters shall never lose their healing virtue.

The kingship over all the earth is where Ellicott parts from the others. Gill takes it of the spiritual reign, with churches set up everywhere and every kind of nation becoming Christian. Clarke says that wherever the knowledge goes the laws of God are acknowledged, and that there shall be only one religion and one form of it, whose essence he states in the two great commandments. Wesley says all shall agree in worshipping one God in one way of spiritual worship. Ellicott holds that the context allows only the narrower sense, all the land rather than all the earth, then makes the concession that keeps the wider reading alive: though this is undoubtedly the prophet's meaning, there is no reason why his words may not have a wider application than he ever contemplated. On the two clauses that follow he improves the rendering to say that the Lord shall be one, glossing it as God being all in all, and that his name shall be one, meaning that he alone shall be worshipped as God.

The levelling of the land and the raising of the city produce a long topographical note and one dissenting translation. Ellicott identifies the two boundary places with their modern names and distances, and distinguishes the southern one from two others of the same name elsewhere; he would render the comparison not as a plain but as the plain, the great rift known by its own name in Hebrew and Arabic, takes the lifting up as figurative of religious prominence, and adds that the name the city bears today, meaning the holy place, is itself a testimony, the nations adopting it acknowledging the city as the fountain-head of religious knowledge. He fixes the four landmarks as the northern, eastern, western and southern limits, covering the whole compass of the city. Clarke renders the first clause differently again, not that the land shall be turned as a plain but that God shall encompass the whole land as a plain, casting his defence around it, and locates the same landmarks with small differences. Wesley reads the levelling agriculturally and then morally, uneven and rocky ground changed into fruitful vineyards, so the church shall be fruitful and humble. Gill keeps it simplest, the encircling mountains made a plain so the city may be seen. On the promise that follows, Clarke says the city shall never be destroyed again, Wesley allows afflictions but no utter wasting, Gill reports a Jewish note that the Messiah comes at this point, and Ellicott would render the word not utter destruction but ban.
12:
The plague on the besiegers is described briefly and referred in three different directions. Gill applies it to the antichristian states and identifies it with one or more of the seven plagues of a later vision. Clarke reads the verse plainly, that all the enemies shall be destroyed and that the effects described are those of famine. Keil and Delitzsch supply the wording without interpretation, a great tumult from the Lord among them so that each lays hold of his neighbour's hand and it rises against him. Wesley explains the mechanism of that tumult, that from murmurs against one another they run at last into civil war and so destroy themselves and avenge the city.

Who does the fighting at Jerusalem is where the readings separate most widely. Gill takes the combatants for the professing people of Christ, the armies of heaven, the chosen and called and faithful who follow the Lamb when he goes out against the antichristian princes. Wesley keeps them entirely historical, the Jews, and suggests that a Maccabean leader may even be intended. Ellicott gives a third account, at once military and psychological: taking courage from the panic that had struck their adversaries, the whole people, not merely those who had escaped out of the city but those outside the walls too, fight once more at Jerusalem, or in its very streets, against a foe he describes as terror-driven, plague-stricken and confounded by God.

The spoil and the beasts are dealt with quickly. Ellicott justifies the wealth gathered by an appeal to practice, that eastern armies always marched with quantities of gold and silver and other valuables, and cites a scriptural instance and a much later one from the campaigns of an Indian emperor. On the plague reaching the animals, Clarke draws a parallel with the cattle and goods struck in Egypt, Ellicott with the beasts destroyed along with a man who had taken forbidden spoil, and Wesley says the creatures the enemy used in war shall by the hand of God be suddenly and strangely destroyed. Gill contributes only a cross-reference about the eating of horseflesh. Keil and Delitzsch, having supplied the wording of these verses, pass straight to the next section and head it as the conversion of the heathen, treating the destruction of the besiegers and the turning of the survivors as a single movement rather than two.
16:
Why the feast of tabernacles in particular is the question the passage raises, and it is answered twice from different directions. Clarke sets it against the other two great festivals, the first commemorating the departure from Egypt and the second the giving of the law, while this one commemorated the forty years of wandering; he thinks it properly brought in to mark the final restoration of the Jews and their establishment in the liberty of the gospel after their long wandering in vice and error. Ellicott gives a liturgical reason instead. The feast is called the feast without qualification, its chief object materially being thanksgiving for the ingathering of harvest and vintage, and on one of its days the Jews always pray that the coming year may not be one of drought; it is therefore fitting that the nations should be shown joining the festival on which the Lord is praised as the beneficent God of nature. He adds the caution that governs his whole reading, that the prophecy is of course not to be taken literally, the prophet foretelling in the language of his own dispensation the future ingathering of the nations. Wesley agrees, taking one festival for all days consecrated to holy worship and finding in the ceremonial usage a shadow of a better. Keil and Delitzsch head the section as the conversion of the heathen. Henry works out what the conversion involves: those left of the enemies of religion, so sensible of their escape that they turn to the worship of the God of Israel, become as much the city's admirers as they had been her adversaries; and he adds that as some of Christ's foes are made his footstool, others are made his friends, their former hostilities pardoned and their services accepted as though they had never fought against the city.

The threat of withheld rain is where the difficulties gather. Gill insists the clause must belong to times preceding the spiritual reign, since in the latter-day glory the rain of the gospel will be on all the earth; he takes Egypt as designating Rome, and refers the whole to the witnesses prophesying in sackcloth who had power to shut heaven. Clarke turns it into a rule of the spiritual life, that those who do not worship God shall not have his blessing and those who neglect the ordinances cannot have the graces dispensed by them, so on such slothful Christians there shall be no rain. Ellicott takes the verse to show that apostasy is not impossible even when worship has become universal, the punishment described in language suited to the symbolic account of the conversion.

On the clause about Egypt having no rain the readings divide sharply. Clarke reads it historically, of Jews who fled persecution, settled in Egypt and built a temple there under a high priest's son, warning that unless they rejoin their brethren they shall have no interest in God's favour. Gill takes the family of Egypt for the Papists, so called for their tyranny and idolatry. Ellicott calls the received rendering impossible and offers two repairs: either the clause is interrogative, asking whether the plague will not fall on them, or, with the old Greek and six Hebrew manuscripts, the negative is dropped so the plague simply falls. He then supplies a geographical argument nobody else makes: if Egypt were punished by a deficiency of water, the country upriver would suffer at the same time even though its people attended the feast, since Egypt can only lack water when the lands to its south do; which he takes as sufficient proof that the prophecy is not literal. Gill notes on the last verse that the word rendered punishment is in the original sin, and that the Targum rightly renders it punishment; Clarke states the conclusion, that God will have his worship established everywhere and non-worshippers lie under his curse.
20:
The inscription on the horses' bells provokes the chapter's most personal note. Clarke observes that bells were formerly hung on horses and camels as they are now, to amuse the animals and encourage them in their work, and then reports what he can see: some very fine Asiatic paintings before him show little bells tied to the legs and larger ones about the necks of horses and mules and camels alike, particularly in a picture of a caravan passing through a valley of serpents on an eastern island he names. He adds that the margin reads bridles rather than bells. He then states the principle the verse carries, that as the gospel is a holy system, preaching holiness and producing it, everything without as well as within bears the same impress, so that a man's labour is begun and continued and ended in the Lord, and even the animals he uses and the instruments he works with are consecrated. Wesley reaches the same conclusion more compactly, that the motto is written as it were on every common thing, that persons bear the dedicating inscription, and that by their study of holiness they make the motto good. Gill dates the whole to a new state of things after the destruction of the antichristian party.

The pots and the bowls are used to measure how far the holiness extends. Wesley draws the gradation carefully: the pots were used in the temple kitchens and were not accounted so sacred as the utensils near the sacrifices and the altar, whereas the bowls received the blood of the sacrifices and were esteemed more holy; the promise is therefore that the holiness of those days shall exceed the holiness of the former. Clarke relays the same comparison from another scholar, that the meanest utensil in the house of God shall be as the vessels of silver and gold used in solemn sacrifice and like the bowls before the altar. Gill supplies a practical reason for the promise, that the sacrifices and sacrificers will be so numerous that the pots in the house will not suffice, so that every pot in city and country must be sanctified and devoted to holy uses. Keil and Delitzsch give the verse without comment.

The Canaanite in the closing clause is identified three ways. Ellicott takes the word as denoting an alien or unbeliever, and gives a modern analogy to convey its force, comparing the way certain national and religious names function as insults among his own contemporaries. Wesley allows both a national and a moral sense, any of the accursed nation, or one who makes merchandise of religion. Clarke commits entirely to the second: the Canaanite is the merchant, and where such are tolerated in a place dedicated to divine worship that place is not the house of the Lord of hosts. He supports it with another scholar's remark that no trafficker shall pollute the house of God as was the custom when the temple was cleansed, and then applies it to his own churches, that collections may be made for the simple purpose of supporting and extending the worship of God but for no other purpose, and especially not on the Lord's day. Wesley ends where the promise does, that all shall know the Lord has the greatest pleasure in upright and sincere love and holiness.
